{{Short description|Theorem in mathematical logic}}

In [[mathematical logic]] and [[computer science]], '''Kamp's theorem''' states that [[linear temporal logic]] is equivalent to the [[monadic first-order logic of order]] over the [[Natural number|non-negative integers]] and the [[Real number|real numbers]]. It is the oldest result in [[Completeness (logic)|expressive completeness]], the study of determining if a given logic can express a desired subject matter. In [[temporal logic]], a logic <math>\mathcal L</math> is expressive complete if every first-order formula with one free variable is equivalent to a formula in <math>\mathcal L</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hodkinson |first1=Ian |last2=Reynolds |first2=Mark |title=Handbook of Modal Logic |chapter=Temporal logic |series=Studies in Logic and Practical Reasoning |date=2007 |volume=3 |pages=655–720 |doi=10.1016/S1570-2464(07)80014-0 |isbn=978-0-444-51690-9 }}</ref> The theorem was proven by [[Hans Kamp]] in his doctoral thesis, ''Tense Logic and the Theory of Linear Order'' (1968).<ref name=":1">{{cite thesis |last=Kamp |first=Johan Anthony Willem |title=Tense Logic and the Theory of Linear Order |date=1968 |publisher=University of California, Los Angeles |oclc=2710894 }}{{pn|date=September 2026}}</ref> In this thesis, Kamp introduces the <math>\mathbf U</math> and <math>\mathbf S</math> operators to [[Arthur Prior|Prior]]'s tense logic,<ref>{{cite book |last=Prior |first=Arthur Norman |title=Time and Modality: Being the John Locke Lectures for 1955-6 Delivered in the University of Oxford |date=1957 |publisher=Oxford |oclc=645151005 }}{{pn|date=September 2026}}</ref> increasing its expressive power and ensuring expressive completeness. Explicitly, Kamp shows that the <math>\mathbf X, \mathbf Y, \mathbf F, \mathbf P</math> operators cannot express <math>\mathbf U</math>.<ref name=":1" />

== Formal Statement ==
A formal statement and proof of Kamp's theorem is provided by Rabinovich.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Rabinovich |first1=Alexander |title=A Proof of Kamp's theorem |journal=Logical Methods in Computer Science |date=18 February 2014 |volume=10 |issue=1 |article-number=730 |doi=10.2168/LMCS-10(1:14)2014 |arxiv=1401.2580 }}</ref> The following is based on his definitions. Let <math>P</math> be a set of atomic predicates.

The syntax for linear temporal logic (LTL) over <math>P</math> is given by the following grammar, where <math>p \in P</math>:

<math>\varphi ::= \top \mid p \mid \neg \varphi \mid \varphi \land \varphi \mid \mathbf X \varphi \mid \mathbf F \varphi \mid \varphi \mathrel \mathbf U \varphi \mid \mathbf Y \varphi \mid \mathbf P \varphi \mid \varphi \mathrel \mathbf S \varphi</math>

An LTL formula is interpreted over a timeline, which is a quadruple <math>\mathcal T = (T, <, s, \mathcal I)</math> given by a set of times <math>T</math>, a [[Total order|linear order]] relation <math><</math> on <math>T</math>, a [[Successor function|successor relation]] <math>s</math> such that <math>(t_1, t_2) \in s</math> if <math>t_2</math> is the successor of <math>t_1</math>, and an [[Structure (mathematical logic)#Interpretation function|interpretation function]] <math>\mathcal I : T \to 2^P</math>. This syntax uses the usual <math>\mathbf X</math> and <math>\mathbf U</math> operators, and includes their past duals, <math>\mathbf Y</math> and <math>\mathbf S</math>, respectively. The satisfaction relation <math>\models</math> is defined as follows, where <math>t \in T</math>:

* <math>\mathcal T, t \models p</math> if <math>p \in \mathcal I(t)</math>
* <math>\mathcal T, t \models \neg \varphi</math> if <math>\mathcal T, t \not\models \varphi</math>
* <math>\mathcal T, t \models \varphi \land \psi </math> if <math>\mathcal T, t \models \varphi</math> and <math>\mathcal T, t \models \psi</math>
* <math>\mathcal T, t \models \mathbf X \varphi </math> if <math>s(t, t + 1)</math> and <math>\mathcal T, t + 1 \models \varphi</math>
* <math>\mathcal T, t \models \mathbf F \varphi </math> if there is <math>t' \geq t</math> such that <math>\mathcal T, t' \models \varphi</math>
* <math>\mathcal T, t \models \varphi \mathrel \mathbf U \psi </math> if there is <math>t' \geq t</math> such that <math>\mathcal T, t' \models \psi</math> and <math>\mathcal T, t'' \models \varphi</math> for all <math>t'' \in [t, t')</math>
* <math>\mathcal T, t \models \mathbf Y \varphi </math> if <math>s(t - 1, t)</math> and <math>\mathcal T, t - 1 \models \varphi</math>
* <math>\mathcal T, t \models \mathbf P \varphi </math> if there is <math>t' \leq t</math> such that <math>\mathcal T, t' \models \varphi</math>
* <math>\mathcal T, t \models \varphi \mathrel \mathbf S \psi </math> if there is <math>t' \leq t</math> such that <math>\mathcal T, t' \models \psi</math> and <math>\mathcal T, t'' \models \varphi</math> for all <math>t'' \in (t', t]</math>

The syntax for monadic first-order logic of order (FOMLO) over <math> P</math> is given by the following grammar, where <math>p \in P</math> and first-order variables are denoted by <math>t</math>:

<math>\varphi ::= t < t \mid t = t \mid p(t) \mid \neg \varphi \mid \varphi \land \varphi \mid \exists x \varphi</math>

The standard [[Structure (mathematical logic)#Satisfaction relation|satisfaction relation]] is used, where <math>\mathcal T, t \models \varphi(x)</math> denotes that <math>\varphi(t)</math> holds.

Let <math>\mathcal T</math> be a timeline such that <math>T</math> is the natural numbers or the real numbers. Kamp's theorem states that every formula in FOMLO is equivalent to a formula in LTL over <math>\mathcal T</math>. That is, for all FOMLO formulas <math>\varphi(x)</math>, there exists an LTL formula <math>\psi</math> such that for all <math>t \in T</math>, <math>\mathcal T, t \models \varphi(x) \iff \mathcal T, t \models \psi</math>. The converse direction is given by the [[standard translation]].

== Other Expressive Completeness Results ==
LTL is not expressively complete over the rationals. Stavi provides the connectives <math>\mathbf U^s</math>and <math>\mathbf S^s</math>such that the logic obtained by extending LTL with these connectives is expressively complete over all linear orders. This result is known as Stavi's theorem.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |last2=Hodkinson |first2=Ian |last3=Reynolds |first3=Mark |title=Temporal Logic: Mathematical Foundations and Computational Aspects |date=1994 |doi=10.1093/oso/9780198537694.001.0001 |isbn=978-0-19-853769-4 }}{{pn|date=September 2026}}</ref>

Unary temporal logic, which is LTL restricted to the operators <math>\mathbf X, \mathbf Y, \mathbf F, \mathbf P</math>, is equivalent to [[Two-variable logic|2-variable FOMLO]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Etessami |first1=Kousha |last2=Vardi |first2=Moshe Y. |last3=Wilke |first3=Thomas |title=First-Order Logic with Two Variables and Unary Temporal Logic |journal=Information and Computation |date=December 2002 |volume=179 |issue=2 |pages=279–295 |doi=10.1006/inco.2001.2953 }}</ref>

[[Metric temporal logic]] is equivalent to the first-order monadic logic of order and metric, <math>FO(<, +\mathbb Q)</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hunter |first1=Paul |last2=Ouaknine |first2=Joel |last3=Worrell |first3=James |title=2013 28th Annual ACM/IEEE Symposium on Logic in Computer Science |chapter=Expressive Completeness for Metric Temporal Logic |date=2013 |pages=349–357 |doi=10.1109/LICS.2013.41 |isbn=978-1-4799-0413-6 }}</ref>

[[Gabbay's separation theorem]] states the separation property is a necessary and sufficient condition for expressive completeness.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov |title=Temporal Logic in Specification |chapter=The declarative past and imperative future |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=1989 |volume=398 |pages=409–448 |doi=10.1007/3-540-51803-7_36 |isbn=978-3-540-51803-7 }}</ref> Kamp's theorem has been proven through pure syntactic, separation and game arguments.<ref name=":0" />
